results.summary: Unilateral lower motor neuron facial palsy has been reported as an early cranial nerve manifestation of acute inflammatory polyradiculoneuropathy in case series, preceding ascending limb weakness by days to two weeks. Subsequent development of global areflexia and limb weakness characterizes an evolving demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy.
results.title: Cranial nerve involvement preceding limb weakness in acute inflammatory polyneuropathy

results.summary: Ill-defined T2 cord signal at the cervicomedullary junction has been documented in severe GBS. Proposed mechanism involves Wallerian degeneration of anterior horn cell axons under severe demyelinating stress. Features reported in association include: absence of a discrete enhancing cord plaque on MRI, albumino-cytologic dissociation without pleocytosis, peripheral demyelinating pattern on NCS, and negative aquaporin-4 antibody.
results.title: Cervical cord T2 signal in acute inflammatory polyneuropathy: Wallerian degeneration versus concomitant myelopathy

output.summary: Facial palsy preceding limb weakness is a recognized early cranial nerve manifestation in a subset of GBS cases. Cervicomedullary junction T2 signal has been reported in severe GBS and is distinguishable from primary transverse myelitis by the absence of a discrete enhancing cord plaque and the presence of peripheral electrodiagnostic features.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start corticosteroids as monotherapy in GBS (steroids may be added if NMOSD / MOGAD is confirmed).
required_recommendations: Brain and cervical spine MRI given cranial nerve involvement and cord T2 signal.

avoided_actions.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.

differential.diagnosis: Bell's palsy with coincident severe neuropathy
differential.key_features: Sequential rather than coincident; preceding Bell's palsy fits early cranial GBS manifestation.

key_clinical_evidence: MRI cord T2 signal can occur in GBS and does not exclude the diagnosis when LMN pattern and CSF dissociation dominate.
Preceding unilateral facial palsy can be the earliest cranial manifestation of GBS.
NMOSD and MOGAD must be excluded by serology before locking in GBS in atypical presentations.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: GBS can show subtle cord T2 changes; the LMN pattern with CSF dissociation and demyelinating EMG remains the dominant evidence.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest transverse myelitis or NMOSD as the primary diagnosis.

Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive ascending weakness over 4 days with global areflexia, bilateral ptosis, and ophthalmoplegia — following 1-week-prior left Bell's palsy. Requiring intubation by day 3.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. R. is a 40-year-old obese woman with hypertension who presented with a 4-day history of bilateral lower extremity numbness and tingling that progressed to weakness over the 24 hours before admission. She had no preceding gastrointestinal or respiratory illness and denied recent vaccination. One week before this admission, she was seen by her primary care physician for left facial weakness involving the forehead and was diagnosed with Bell's palsy; she was started on a prednisone taper and valacyclovir. On admission, she was afebrile (temperature 99.2°F), blood pressure was 167/78 mm Hg, and she was tachycardic at 104 bpm. Neurological examination showed left lower facial weakness in an LMN distribution consistent with the prior Bell's palsy diagnosis, motor strength 4/5 in the upper extremities and 3/5 in the lower extremities bilaterally, globally absent deep tendon reflexes, a negative Hoffmann sign, and decreased light touch and cold sensation below C5 bilaterally. Extraocular movements were intact on day 1 and nystagmus was absent. There was no bowel dysfunction. She had no encephalopathy and was oriented throughout. On hospital day 2, her strength declined precipitously to 2/5 in all four extremities, she developed bilateral ptosis and urinary incontinence, and she demonstrated early respiratory compromise with SpO2 dropping to 94% on room air. On day 3, bilateral ptosis worsened markedly, ophthalmoplegia developed with limited elevation and abduction bilaterally, and she demonstrated prominent nystagmus — upbeat on upgaze and downbeat on downgaze. She required emergency intubation for worsening respiratory failure. The rapid progression from the Bell's palsy diagnosis to quadriplegia and respiratory failure over 10 days, combined with global areflexia and bilateral cranial nerve involvement, raised urgent concern for a severe acute neuromuscular process. Aquaporin-4 antibody was sent immediately given the MRI cord signal change.

neurological_exam.additional: Patient had left facial weakness diagnosed as Bell's palsy by primary care 1 week before admission. Lower extremity numbness and tingling began 4 days before admission; weakness 1 day before. Admitted on day 1 with temperature 99.2°F, BP 167/78, otherwise normal vitals. By day 2 she developed urinary incontinence and bilateral ptosis. Day 3 respiratory failure required emergency intubation. No prior history of demyelinating disease. Aquaporin-4 antibody sent and negative. MRI cervical spine showed T2 cord signal change extending to cervicomedullary junction — initially concerning for transverse myelitis but MRI head was normal.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Day 1: Left lower facial weakness involving forehead — LMN pattern (Bell's palsy diagnosed 1 week prior). Extraocular movements intact, nystagmus absent. Day 2: bilateral ptosis appeared. Day 3: bilateral ptosis worsened significantly, ophthalmoplegia developed (limited elevation and abduction bilaterally), prominent nystagmus — upbeat on upgaze, downbeat on downgaze.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4 throughout hospitalization. No encephalopathy. Normal cognitive testing.
neurological_exam.motor: Day 1 admission: UE 4/5 bilateral, LE 3/5 bilateral. Day 2: declined to 2/5 all extremities. Day 3: effectively quadriplegic — required intubation for respiratory failure.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Globally absent deep tendon reflexes bilaterally throughout admission. No Hoffmann sign. No Babinski.
